newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Juppe, arts elite lock horns on far right.
newsitem.headline: France's Juppe, arts elite lock horns on far right.

text.p: Prime Minister Alain Juppe locked horns with France's artistic and intellectual elite over an immigration bill on Monday, as both sides accused the other of playing into the hands of the extreme right.

More than 3,000 film-makers, actors, writers and academics have urged civil disobedience over the draft bill sanctioned by the centre-right government, which they say mirrors the ideas of the far-right, anti-immigration National Front.
"These (petitions) are serious acts because they undermine the state and democracy," Juppe told RTL radio.
He ruled out any softening of the bill which requires French citizens to report the departure of any foreigners, most of whom come from the developing world, staying at their home.

"The role of intellectuals is to lobby for the truth, not to obscure it. It is also a blow against our policy of integration...Many people don't want to distinguish between legal and illegal immigration. They are doing the work of those who advocate xenophobia," he said.

Protests have included separate lists of hundreds of scientists, doctors and lawyers calling on the public to flout the new law if it is approved by parliament later this month. Actresses Jeanne Moreau and Catherine Deneuve, and film-makers Bernard Tavernier and Mathieu Kassovitz are all signatories.

The rebels gained some support from the political establishment on Monday. Socialist Lionel Jospin, leader of the biggest opposition force, stopped short of calling for civil disobedience but threw his weight behind the protesters.

"The Prime Minister would be wise to take a step back, especially on the (guests' departure) provision...In any case, we will take several measures of the bill to the (watchdog) Constitutional Council," Jospin told the daily Le Monde.
Communist chief Robert Hue earlier urged leftist parties to back the intellectuals, saying the government was trying to encourage informing, which harked back to wartime collaboration.
Jeannette Gaschard, independent mayor of Maironnes in south-west France, pledged to disobey the law because she did not want the townfolk turned into "potential police officers".

The left-leaning daily Liberation published 3,000 signatures from the intellectual and arts elite, alongside 54 drawings by leading cartoonists. One showed Asterix the Gaul kicking over a cauldron marked "Marechal here we are", a rallying cry for wartime collaborationist leader Marechal Philippe Petain.

"Since the Right returned to power four years ago...it has given only one answer to the rise of the National Front: a harder, more restrictive stance, meaning fewer freedoms," Le Monde said in an editorial.

The bill will require people supplying certificates to foreigners saying they will take responsibility for them during their stay in France also to declare when their guests leave. Juppe denied it provided for any register of foreigners.

Would-be visitors from many Third World countries who cannot show they have enough money to fund a long visit to France are currently granted visas only if they can provide a certificate showing someone in France will provide them with lodging.

The new article, like the certificates before them, are aimed at discouraging would-be illegal immigrants of which there are an estimated one million in France. There are a further four million foreigners legally resident in the country.
An IPSOS opinion poll for the daily Le Figaro showed that 66 percent of voters distanced themselves from the National Front's ideas on immigration, against 28 percent who did not.
